The **anymake** skill is the hub of the Anymake build system -- an agentic build system that takes any software idea from conception to a finished, shipped result through a phased, artifact-driven process.

## Purpose

Anymake's purpose is to take any software idea -- SaaS, CLI, library, API, internal tool, static site, or hobby project -- from conception to a finished, shipped result. It uses a phased, artifact-driven process that adapts to what you're building.

## Trigger Phrases

The skill triggers on:
- "start a new project"
- "continue my build"
- "plan a product"
- "build an app"
- "Anymake"
- "agentic build"
- "structured build process"
- "I have a product idea"
- "launch a SaaS"
- "yolo mode"
- "autonomous mode"
- "--yolo"
- "build autonomously"
- Working on any new product development

## Core Philosophy

- **You** own the vision, make all product and business decisions, and approve every phase gate
- **Claude** executes everything: researches, plans, builds, deploys -- within approved scope
- **Artifacts** are the only source of truth -- conversation memory is ephemeral, documents are permanent
- **Checkpoints** gate every phase transition -- no skipping, no shortcuts
- **Project type drives everything** -- chosen at the start and governs which phases run, which questions get asked, the Phase 4 build order, and the gate criteria
- **The success model is first-class** -- every project defines what success means up front and designs for it from Phase 0
- **Visual quality is first-class for user-facing products** -- anything with screens shown to others must look like it was built by a funded company, not a tutorial

## Phase Overview

| Phase | Name | Output | Gate |
|-------|------|--------|------|
| 0 | Foundation | `PROJECT.md` -- identity, scope, revenue model, success definition | your approval |
| 1 | Discovery | `docs/01-discovery.md` -- market, competitors, users, risks | your approval |
| 2 | Planning | PRD + UX + Architecture + Monetization | your approval |
| 3 | Solutioning | Epics, stories, ordered backlog | your approval |
| 4 | Implementation | Production code, CI/CD, security reviewed, staging deployed | your approval |
| 5 | Launch | Live product, metrics dashboard, growth loop | Ongoing |

This table shows the `saas` default. Other project types reshape it -- skipping phases or sub-tracks, or replacing Launch entirely. The active type's guide in `PROJECT_TYPES/[project_type]/guide.md` governs.

## Session Startup Ritual

Every session follows this ritual:
1. Check `PROJECTS/[name]/PHASE_STATE.md` -- if it doesn't exist, start Phase 0
2. Read `PROJECT_TYPES/[project_type]/manifest.md` and `guide.md` -- these govern the session
3. Identify current phase + current step
4. Read the step's detailed instructions from the type's guide
5. Execute exactly one step -- completely (suspended in autonomous mode)
6. Produce the concrete artifact or decision for that step
7. Update `PHASE_STATE.md`
8. Report: what was done, what needs your eyes, what's next

## Behavioral Rules

1. One step per session -- complete it fully before reporting (suspended in autonomous mode)
2. One artifact at a time -- finish one document before starting the next
3. Recommend, don't list -- "I recommend X because Y" not "here are 5 options"
4. Scope is a hard boundary -- nothing gets built outside approved scope
5. Clean exits -- every session ends with PHASE_STATE.md updated and next step named
6. Success model is first-class -- defined in Phase 0 per the project type
7. Autonomous mode gates -- when `autonomous_mode: true`, spawn the Product Owner Proxy at every phase gate instead of waiting for user input; security failures always escalate to the real user

## Autonomous Mode (Yolo)

Activated by `--yolo`, `yolo mode`, `autonomous mode`, or `build autonomously`. When activated, `autonomous_mode: true` is set in PHASE_STATE.md, and the system proceeds through all phases without stopping at user approval gates, spawning the Product Owner Proxy to evaluate each gate. The proxy approves clean artifacts and returns specific required changes for incomplete ones. Security failures always escalate to the real user regardless of mode.

## Companion Skills

Anymake is a skill suite with 10 companion skills that handle specific workflow steps:
- `anymake-build-loop` (Phase 4, Step 4.3)
- `anymake-experience-setup` (Phase 3, Step 3.2b)
- `anymake-experience-check` (Phase 4, Step 4.6)
- `anymake-design-system` (Phase 2, Step 2.2b)
- `anymake-security-review` (Phase 4, Step 4.5)
- `anymake-deploy` (Phase 4 staging, Phase 5.2)
- `anymake-brownfield` (existing-code path)
- `anymake-iterate` (Phase 5.6 onward)
- `anymake-agile` (post-launch bug/feature pipeline)
- `anymake-new-type` (extending the type system)

The hub routes; companions execute. Companions read the same `PROJECT_TYPES/<id>/manifest.md`, `PHASE_STATE.md`, and templates, so state and conventions never fork.

The **anymake-agile** skill is the single post-launch front door for changing any product Anymake has already built. Its full title is "From 'This Button Isn't Working' to a Reviewed, Reverted-able Fix." It replaces ad-hoc troubleshooting with a disciplined pipeline: **understand, track, design, review, approve, build, verify**.

## When to Use

- The user reports something broken on a built project: "such-and-such button isn't working correctly," "I'm seeing an error when..."
- The user requests a feature or change: "add SSO," "change the export format," "remove the trial banner," "now I want it to also..."
- `anymake-iterate` has picked the next increment and it's time to define and build it
- Directly: "log an issue," "report a bug," "run the agile flow on this"

## Trigger Phrases

"[X] isn't working," "I found a bug," "this button is broken," "add a feature," "change how X works," "remove Y," "now I want it to...," "feature request," "log an issue"

## The Four Promises

1. The shipped change **fixes the reported issue / delivers the requested feature, actually driven and confirmed** -- not an adjacent guess
2. It **breaks nothing else** -- blast radius mapped and regression-tested before build
3. New UI **looks designed-in from day one** -- checked against the design system
4. Everything is **traceable and revertible** -- issue to plan to branch to merge SHA to revert command

## The Cast

| Role | Definition | Owns |
|------|------------|------|
| Main agent (you) | this skill | Intake with the reporter, issue tracking, orchestration, state |
| **Solution Architect** | `AGENTS/solution-architect.md` | Full-project review + the Development Plan. Never touches code |
| **Plan Reviewer** | `AGENTS/plan-reviewer.md` | Adversarial review of the plan. Fresh context each round; never edits the plan |
| Cartographer | `AGENTS/cartographer.md` | Refreshing the intent layer before design, and after merge |
| Build engine | `anymake-build-loop` | Building the approved stories with full traceability |

Architect and Reviewer **must be separate sub-agents** -- the thing that designs is never the thing that approves.

## The Pipeline

### 1. Intake -- understand before anything
Capture the reporter's words verbatim. Ask minimum questions to pin it down. Attempt to reproduce. Restate the issue in system terms (using `docs/SYSTEM_MAP.md`) and get explicit confirmation.

### 2. Track -- a labeled issue in the project's repo
Create a GitHub issue using `TEMPLATES/issue.md` and `gh issue create`, with labels for type (`type:bug`/`type:feature`/`type:chore`), severity (`severity:critical`/`severity:major`/`severity:minor`), and status lifecycle (`status:intake` through closed or `status:escalated`).

### 3. Solution -- spawn the Solution Architect
Ensure the intent layer is fresh (spawn the Cartographer if needed). Then spawn the Solution Architect to review the whole project and write `issue-[N]/plan.md`. If it reports an intent conflict, run the intent conflict gate before proceeding.

### 4. Review loop -- independent approval or specific objections
Spawn a fresh Plan Reviewer each round. It returns `NEEDS CHANGES` (re-spawn Architect), `ESCALATE` (straight to user), or `APPROVED` (proceed). After the 3rd `NEEDS CHANGES`, escalate to the user.

### 5. Approval gate
Normal mode: present summary and wait for user approval. Autonomous mode: spawn Product Owner Proxy. Security-relevant plans always go to the real user.

### 6. Execute -- through the engine, with traceability
Feed the plan's stories to `anymake-build-loop`. Branch `issue/[N]-[slug]`, every commit references `#[N]`, PR body says `Closes #[N]`. Record base SHA before merge, merge SHA + tag + revert command after.

### 7. Verify & close
The build loop's Experience Runner pass is the primary evidence. For UI changes, run the design system audit. Ask the reporter to confirm. Close the issue with merge SHA, tag, revert command, and experience report path. Spawn the Cartographer to refresh the intent layer.

## Guardrails

- No code before an approved plan -- not even for "obvious" one-liners
- Architect and Reviewer are always separate sub-agent contexts
- The issue is the scope -- adjacent ideas go to `PARKING_LOT.md`
- Security always reaches the real user regardless of mode
- The paper trail is the product -- a stranger should be able to audit or undo any change from the issue alone

The **anymake-brownfield** skill is the on-ramp for bringing Anymake's phased discipline to an **existing codebase** instead of starting from a greenfield idea. It reverse-engineers the Phase 0-3 artifacts from code that already exists so the hub can resume at Phase 4 (or wherever appropriate) with real state.

## When to Use

- The user points Anymake at an existing repository
- Mid-build adoption: "we have an MVP, take it from here"
- Before any other companion skill can run on a repo that has no `PROJECTS/[name]/` workspace yet

## Trigger Phrases

"Adopt Anymake in this repo," "onboard an existing project," "reverse-engineer a PRD," "Anymake an existing codebase," "I already have code," "continue building on top of what's here"

## What It Produces

It reuses the same templates and locations as the hub -- no parallel formats:

| Artifact | Template | Derived from |
|----------|----------|--------------|
| `PROJECTS/[name]/PROJECT.md` | `TEMPLATES/project.md` | README, package metadata, code purpose, inferred success model |
| `PROJECTS/[name]/docs/01-discovery.md` (lite) | `TEMPLATES/discovery.md` | What the product clearly is + obvious competitors/risks (mark assumptions) |
| `PROJECTS/[name]/docs/architecture-map.md` | `TEMPLATES/adr.md` | Actual stack, structure, data model, integrations -- each ADR marked "as-built" |
| `PROJECTS/[name]/BACKLOG` (epics + stories) | `TEMPLATES/epic.md`, `TEMPLATES/story.md` | Gaps, TODOs, requested features, tech debt |
| Experience Scripts for the backlog | `TEMPLATES/experience-script.md` (via `anymake-experience-setup`, retrofit mode) | Closes the Experience Script gap for stories that never went through Phase 3 |
| `docs/environment.md` | `TEMPLATES/environment.md` (via `anymake-experience-setup`) | How the existing app actually starts locally |
| `PROJECTS/[name]/PHASE_STATE.md` | `TEMPLATES/phase-state.md` | Set `project_type`, `autonomous_mode`, and the resume point |

## The Engineering-Intent Layer

Brownfield's map *is* the first run of the engineering-intent layer. The system map, as-built ADRs, and invariants reverse-engineered here are exactly what the Cartographer (`AGENTS/cartographer.md`) maintains going forward. Once onboarded, future changes go through `anymake-agile`, which reads this layer and keeps it current.

## Procedure

1. **Detect type.** Inspect the repo and recommend a `project_type`; confirm with one question. Read `PROJECT_TYPES/<id>/manifest.md`.
2. **Map the system.** Survey structure, stack, data model, external integrations, build/test/deploy setup.
3. **Reverse-engineer PROJECT.md.** Identity, scope, and the success model. Flag inferred items.
4. **Discovery snapshot (lite).** Capture market position, obvious competitors, and live risks. Mark unknowns.
5. **As-built ADRs.** Record significant architecture decisions already made, each marked `Status: as-built`.
6. **Forward backlog.** Turn gaps, TODOs, known bugs, and requested features into epics and stories.
6a. **Retrofit the Experience Harness.** Run `anymake-experience-setup` in retrofit mode to author Experience Scripts for every story and write `docs/environment.md`.
7. **Write PHASE_STATE.md** and set the resume point (usually Phase 3 approval into Phase 4).

## Guardrails

- Don't rewrite working code during onboarding -- this phase is read-and-document only
- Mark every inference -- reverse-engineered intent is a hypothesis until the user confirms
- Respect the existing architecture in as-built ADRs; propose changes as new backlog items
- One artifact at a time, ending with PHASE_STATE.md updated

The **anymake-build-loop** skill is the autonomous build engine at the heart of Anymake's Phase 4 Implementation. Given an ordered backlog of stories with acceptance criteria, it builds them one at a time through a strict five-stage loop: **Orchestrator, Planner, Worker, Validator, Experience Runner**.

## When to Use

- The hub invokes this at **Phase 4, Step 4.3** once the backlog from Phase 3 is approved
- Directly, on any repo that has a runnable dev environment and an ordered list of stories with testable acceptance criteria

## Trigger Phrases

"Run the build loop," "implement my backlog," "build these stories," "agentic build," "start the worker/validator loop"

## The Five Stages

| Stage | Definition | Role |
|-------|------------|------|
| **Orchestrator** | `AGENTS/orchestrator.md` | Reads backlog + dependency graph, maintains `BOARD.md`, dispatches agents, enforces policies, escalates. Never writes feature code. |
| **Planner** | `AGENTS/planner.md` | Receives ONE story ID, translates it into a self-contained task brief (`TEMPLATES/task-brief.md`), including a section 3a Experience Script. Never writes code. |
| **Worker** | `AGENTS/worker.md` | Receives the approved task brief, implements in strict layer order (the type's manifest Build Order), commits each layer, opens a PR, and appends any new pattern to `CONVENTIONS.md`. |
| **Validator** | `AGENTS/validator.md` | Checks every acceptance criterion against the implementation, runs the security checklist, defers Human-Only criteria with section 3a coverage to the Experience Runner. Returns PASS / FAIL / ESCALATE. |
| **Experience Runner** | `AGENTS/experience-runner.md` | Checks out the branch, launches the real app per `docs/environment.md`, and executes every scenario in the task brief's section 3a -- clicking, typing, running commands, sending requests -- comparing actual results to scripted expectations. Returns PASS / FAIL / ESCALATE. |

**Each stage MUST be a separate sub-agent.** Collapsing all five into one context defeats the architecture -- this is the cardinal anti-pattern.

## How to Run It

1. Set up the board -- copy `TEMPLATES/BOARD.md` to `PROJECTS/[name]/BOARD.md` with every story as a card in `Backlog`
2. Become the Orchestrator -- load `AGENTS/orchestrator.md` and follow it
3. Per ready story: spawn a Planner sub-agent for the task brief, check completeness, spawn a Worker
4. Per PR: spawn a Validator; it returns PASS / FAIL / ESCALATE
5. Per Validator PASS (unless section 3a is N/A): spawn an Experience Runner to launch and drive the app
6. Apply policies from `AGENTS/arbiter.md`: retry matrix, PR review rules (PRs #1-3 and ADR-touching PRs always require human review), escalation lexicon
7. Update `BOARD.md` after every agent action
8. Loop until the backlog is empty or an ESCALATE blocks progress

## Key Inputs

- Ordered backlog + dependency graph from Phase 3
- `project_type` manifest for Build Order and gate deltas
- `docs/environment.md` for how the Experience Runner launches the app
- Agent definitions from `AGENTS/`
- Templates from `TEMPLATES/`

## Done When

Every story is `Done` on the board, every merged PR passed validation **and** its Experience Runner check (or was explicitly N/A), and the run log + escalations are recorded in `BOARD.md`. Then the hub proceeds to Phase 4 Step 4.5 (security review) and 4.6 (staging review).

## Anti-Patterns

- Orchestrator-as-worker (one context doing all five stages)
- Skipping layers in the build order
- Merging a PR on a Validator PASS alone, without an Experience Runner PASS
- Waiving a Human-Only criterion without an Experience Runner ever driving it
- Merging PRs #1-3 without human review
- "No test suite" as a result -- every story with runtime-verifiable criteria gets automated tests

The Phase 4 Build Order is one of the most important type-specific settings in Anymake. It defines the **exact layer sequence that Workers follow** when building each story, and it overrides the SaaS default for every other type. Here is how each type's build order differs:

## SaaS (the reference)
`Schema -> Migration -> API -> Component -> Page -> Integration -> Test`

The full web stack, top to bottom: database first, then the API that reads it, then the UI components and pages that call the API, then integrations, then tests.

## Hobby
`Data/State -> Core logic -> Interface (UI or CLI) -> Tests (optional)`

Adapts to shape. Simplified -- skip layers that don't apply. Tests are optional.

## CLI
`Core logic -> CLI layer (arg/flag parsing) -> I/O & formatting -> Tests -> Packaging/Distribution -> Docs (README + usage)`

No schema/migration/frontend. Core logic is pure and importable (no `argv` dependency), the CLI layer is thin on top, tests assert exit codes specifically, and packaging/distribution is a first-class layer.

## Library
`Public API & types -> Core implementation -> Tests (high coverage -- the contract) -> Docs & examples -> Packaging (build outputs, exports map) -> CI (test matrix across supported versions)`

No schema/frontend. The public API shape is settled before any logic fills in behind it. Tests are the priority (high coverage of every public export is non-negotiable). Docs and packaging are release deliverables, not afterthoughts.

## API Service
`Schema -> Migration -> API (routes/handlers/services) -> Integration (third-party, webhooks) -> Tests (contract + behavior)`

The SaaS order minus the frontend: no Component or Page layers. Tests cover both the contract (responses match schemas) and behavior (correct results, auth enforced, rate limits work).

## Internal Tool
`Schema -> Migration -> API -> Component -> Page -> Integration -> Test`

Same as SaaS, minus the payment milestone. The build order is identical because internal tools are full web apps -- they just aren't sold.

## Static Site
`Design system / layout & components -> Pages & content -> SEO & meta (titles, descriptions, OG, sitemap, robots) -> Forms & integrations (analytics, newsletter) -> Checks (Lighthouse, broken links, responsive) -> Deploy`

No schema/migration/API/auth. Content and SEO are the work. Checks (Lighthouse, broken links, responsive) are a formal layer before deploy.

## Agentic Harness
`Contracts -> Backend adapters -> Stage-graph engine -> Agent runner/sandbox -> Per-stage AgentSpecs -> Tracing -> Control plane -> Dashboard -> Integration tests -> Deploy`

The most unique build order. 10 layers. Contracts (typed schemas) come first because everything is built against them. The engine exists before any agent. Per-stage agents are built one at a time, simplest first, to prove the loop end-to-end before investing in every stage's prompt engineering.

## Key Insight

The build order ensures **each layer builds on the last** -- no hidden dependencies, no skipping ahead. The Worker agent reads the active type's manifest to get the right order, so switching types changes the build sequence automatically.

In Anymake, the `saas` type is the **reference** -- the default gate criteria in `AGENTS/product-owner-proxy.md` are written for `saas`. All other types express their gates as **deltas** (skip, replace, add, keep, relax) against this baseline. Here is how each type modifies the gates:

## SaaS (baseline -- no deltas)
The default gate criteria apply in full. All monetization checks, prototype gate, market-size checks, AARRR metrics, legal requirements, and security checks are active.

## Hobby
- **Skip:** All monetization checks, mandatory prototype gate, market-size/competitor checks, GDPR/legal, AARRR metrics, mandatory ADR set
- **Relax:** Automated-test mandate (tests recommended but gate does not fail solely for missing tests). Same relaxation for Experience Script coverage.
- **Keep:** Scope clarity (Phase 0), "it actually runs" as Phase 4 bar, no-secrets-in-code

## CLI
- **Skip:** Monetization (unless chosen), market-size depth, GUI-prototype gate, GDPR/legal, AARRR metrics
- **Replace:** Prototype gate -> **CLI UX check** (help text exists and is clear, usage examples, consistent error messages and exit codes)
- **Add:** Install verification (published artifact installs and runs on a clean environment), usage docs present
- **Keep:** Acceptance-criteria quality, test coverage for runtime behavior, no-secrets-in-code

## Library
- **Skip:** Monetization (unless chosen), market-size depth, GUI prototype, GDPR/legal, AARRR metrics, auth/hosting ADRs
- **Replace:** Prototype gate -> **public-API design review** (signatures and types documented and ergonomic)
- **Add:** Strong test-coverage requirement (every public export needs tests), docs/examples for every public export, semver/release process defined
- **Keep:** Acceptance-criteria quality, no-secrets-in-code, dependency justification

## API Service
- **Skip:** GUI-prototype gate; monetization unless paid model chosen
- **Replace:** Prototype gate -> **API contract review** (every endpoint has request/response schema, status codes, example; error format consistent)
- **Add:** Rate-limiting on public endpoints, auth required on all non-public routes, versioning strategy defined
- **Keep:** All security checks **heightened** (this is an attack surface), acceptance-criteria quality, test coverage, no-secrets-in-code

## Internal Tool
- **Skip:** All monetization checks, market-size/competitor checks, public-launch legal, AARRR metrics
- **Relax:** Prototype is recommended, not a hard gate
- **Replace:** Success metrics -> adoption / time-saved targets instead of revenue
- **Keep:** Auth + authorization checks (internal data still needs protection), acceptance-criteria quality, test coverage, no-secrets-in-code

## Static Site
- **Skip:** Auth/database checks (unless needed), monetization unless chosen
- **Keep (hard):** Prototype/visual-quality gate -- design quality is the deliverable
- **Add:** SEO baseline (title + meta description per page, OG tags, sitemap + robots), Core Web Vitals targets, responsive at mobile/tablet/desktop
- **Keep:** Content-quality standard (no placeholders), accessibility, no-secrets-in-code

## Agentic Harness
- **Skip:** GUI-prototype gate for pipeline; monetization unless charging; AARRR; public-launch legal
- **Replace:** Prototype gate -> **Pipeline dry-run review** (one synthetic work item end-to-end)
- **Add:** (1) Declarative stage graph, (2) schema-validated output per stage, (3) credential isolation, (4) atomic claim under concurrent workers, (5) complete end-to-end trace, (6) cost cap/circuit breaker, (7) control plane with pause/resume/step
- **Keep:** All security checks **heightened** -- LLM-directed code execution with tool access

## Key Principle

When a manifest says a check is **skipped**, the Product Owner Proxy must not fail a gate for it. When it says **replaced**, the proxy applies the replacement check instead. This ensures each type gets the right level of rigor for what it actually is.

The **project type is set once** when the project is created. It is recorded as `project_type` in `PROJECTS/[name]/PHASE_STATE.md` and read at the start of every session. The hub skill states: "Chosen once at project creation, stored as `project_type` in `PHASE_STATE.md`, and read at the start of every session."

## Why It's Set Once

The project type governs *everything*:
- Which phases run (full, lite, skipped, replaced)
- What questions get asked in each phase
- The Phase 4 build order
- The gate criteria (what the Product Owner Proxy checks)
- The success model (revenue vs. adoption vs. personal use vs. API quality)
- Which companion skills apply (design system? monetization? CLI UX?)

Changing the type mid-build would invalidate artifacts already produced under the old type's rules -- a PRD written for a CLI command spec is not a SaaS feature list, and a hobby project's simple checklist backlog is not a SaaS epic structure.

## But Projects Do Outgrow Their Type

The guides explicitly acknowledge this. The `hobby` guide says: "If it grows into something you want to ship for real, switch `project_type` to `saas` (or `cli`/`library`) and pick up the heavier phases from there. The work so far carries over."

The `cli` guide says: "If the tool grows a GUI or a hosted, monetized surface, that's a signal it has outgrown `cli` -- switch types and the fuller phases (prototype gate, monetization, AARRR) kick in."

The `internal-tool` guide says: "If this tool ever needs to be sold outside the company, switch `project_type` to `saas` and the monetization, market, and public-launch phases activate."

## How to Switch

The practical path is to use the **`anymake-brownfield`** skill on your existing codebase with the new project type:

1. Update `project_type` in `PHASE_STATE.md` to the new type
2. Invoke `anymake-brownfield` to reverse-engineer the new type's required artifacts from your existing code
3. It will identify gaps (e.g., switching from `hobby` to `saas` means you now need monetization design, a prototype gate, AARRR metrics, legal pages, full architecture ADRs)
4. It creates a forward backlog of everything needed to satisfy the new type's requirements
5. Resume the normal flow under the new type's guide

The existing code carries over -- brownfield doesn't rewrite working code, it documents what exists and plans what's missing under the new type's rules.

## Summary

- Project type is set once at creation and should not be changed casually
- When a project legitimately outgrows its type, use `anymake-brownfield` to transition
- The work done under the old type carries over; the brownfield skill gaps-fills the new type's requirements
